newsitem.title: USA: Delta Air sets $15 billion Boeing deal.
newsitem.headline: Delta Air sets $15 billion Boeing deal.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc. Thursday named Boeing Co. as its exclusive aircraft supplier for the next quarter-century in a landmark deal that could be worth more than $15 billion.

Ending months of speculation about its purchasing plans, Delta announced $6.7 billion in firm orders for 106 Boeing aircraft -- 70 new-generation 737s, five 757s, 10 767-300s and 21 767-400s -- through the year 2006.

The agreement, similar to a plan already in place between Boeing and American Airlines, also calls for 124 options on other aircraft, including 10 options on the new Boeing wide-body 777 aircraft. Another 414 rolling options would bring the total number of Boeing aircraft involved to 644.

Options are guaranteed delivery slots while rolling options are delivery positions that replace options as they are exercised or expire. Delta said both the options and the rolling options covered aircraft deliveries through 2018.
The first delivery was set for next spring and would comprise 767-400 aircraft needed to replace Delta's ageing fleet of Lockheed L-1011s.

Delta said separately it placed an $800 million order with CFM International of Evandale, Ohio, for engines for the new 737s, which were scheduled for delivery starting in mid-1998. CFM is a joint venture of General Electric Co. and Snecma of France.

"This flexible and disciplined fleet acquisition plan gives us the right aircraft at the right time and at the right price to build on Delta's competitive advantages as we put our global strategy in place," Delta Chief Executive Ron Allen said during a news conference at the headquarters of the nation's third largest airline.
"We can manage deliveries while providing significant long-term price control," he said.
Although the formal agreement covers 20 years, Allen said it would likely meet Delta's fleet acquisition needs for the next 25 to 30 years.

Committing to a single manufacturer allows Delta to streamline its fleet and reduce maintenance and training costs. The plan will also allow Delta to retire its older aircraft, lowering operating costs.

Delta Executive Vice President Harry Alger said Boeing faced intense competition from European aircraft consortium Airbus Industrie. But the Seattle-based company, the world's largest maker of commercial aircraft, won on start-up costs and order flexibility, Delta said.
"With Boeing, we have developed a true partnership," Alger said.
Airbus officials did not return calls to the group's offices in New York.
"This is a remarkably significant event for us," said Ron Woodard, president of the Boeing Commercial Aircraft Division, which has made about 330 aircraft for Delta over the past 30 years.

"With the type of partnership we're entering into now, we really have a shared destiny and what is important for us at Boeing is that Delta be successful. I think we have a relationship coming where we're going to be much more closely linked at all levels."
Industry experts said Boeing could be expected to pursue similar deals with other airlines.

"I would guess Boeing would be prepared to replicate these two deals with anyone who was interested if they were big enough," said Barbara Beyer, president of Avmark Inc., an aviation consulting firm.
"It gives them a guaranteed source of income and shuts out their competitor, and that's worth a lot of discount."

The order, which would make Delta the airline to launch Boeing's 767-400, the next generation of 767 wide-body aircraft, concentrates on domestic jetliners. Delta said it would continue to evaluate its international aircraft needs.

Delta said it plans to maintain the ability to pay for the aircraft with internally generated funds, while still meeting financial goals for annual profit margins, lower debt and an investment-grade rating for its debt.
Delta said the plan is based on internal capacity growth of about 2 percent a year through 2002.
Boeing stock rose $1 to $105 and Delta slipped 12.5 cents to $84.375, both in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange. GE lost 87.5 cents to $102.625, also on the NYSE.
